utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-00-39-&-40-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Nicola Piacente and Carolyn Edgerton, for the Prosecution, assisted by Carmela Annink-Javier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, Deyan Brasich for the Krajisnik Defence. I'm aided by Mr. Goran Neskovic of the Bosnia and Herzegovinac bar, as well as by Mr. Karkin Fahrija, also of that bar. Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Robert Pavich on behalf of Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Robert Pavich on behalf of Bilijana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The purpose of this hearing is to work on the progress of this case. I should say that I have to attend a meeting of the Bureau at five o’clock so we need to be expeditious, if you please. I think the easiest way to deal with it is this, that the Trial Chamber has drawn up a timetable. It's a prospective timetable, but we would expect it largely to be adhered to. I will hear what counsel, of course, have got to say about it, but it might be simplest if the legal officer or somebody would kindly distribute the proposed timetable. Just one for the Prosecution and one each for the Defence. You will see, first of all, that the proposed trial date is the second half of November. That is because this trial cannot take place before the new Judges have been installed and the Trial Chambers have been reconstituted. But with that in mind, this Trial Chamber -- this trial should clearly take place as soon after that event as possible, bearing in mind that one of the accused has been in custody for nearly a year already. Bearing in mind too that the other accused has more recently come and, therefore, should have time for preparation of the trial. This will be a substantial trial, and the Trial Chamber has in mind the difficulties of preparation for both sides, but also the need that the trial should take place as soon as possible in order that times in custody are kept to a minimum before trial. With those considerations in mind, it's necessary to give as much time as possible for reasonable preparation, and the proposed timetable, you'll see, is there should be a further conference on the 17th of May; that the Prosecution should complete disclosure by the 22nd of June; pre-trial brief, 29th of June. Pausing there, that will allow the Prosecution three months from today's date to be ready. I will hear any submissions on that, but in my view, they should be ready by now considering the amount of time that has elapsed since this indictment was first preferred and since the first accused came into custody. That would be followed by a Status Conference at the beginning of July, another one at the beginning of September. The Defence Pre-Trial briefs would then be on the 28th of September. Pausing there, that will have allowed the Defence a period of three months between the Prosecution Pre-Trial brief and the submission of their own briefs. A Pre-Trial Conference would then be scheduled for the 5th of November and an earlier Status Conference on the 3rd of October. All that should lead to the trial being ready, this case being trial-ready, by the second half of November of this year. Now, I'm sorry that you haven't had greater notice of this proposed timetable, but it's important that we get on with it. And so I'll hear any submissions that anybody has about it, and after that, we will deal with any other matters, bearing in mind the constraints of time. Now, Mr. Piacente, it seems to me that the 29th of June is the very latest that the Prosecution can have for their Pre-Trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I cannot share the same opinion, considering the warning scenario this case has developed in the last month. The previously appointed senior trial attorney, Ms. Brenda Hollis, left the OTP, and the newly appointed senior trial attorney, Mark Harmon, is engaged in the Trial Chamber dealing with the Krstic case. There will be the need to restructure the whole trial team, considering the fact that I myself will be leaving the OTP by the end of May. So I would say, reconsidering, reading what Your Honour submitted to both parties, I would say that the Prosecution can be ready to disclose the bulk, the biggest part, of the material falling within the language of 65 ter (E) by the first week of July. We will try the best, beyond best, to finish, to be ready with the Pre-Trial brief by the fall of this year, 2001, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Piacente, you are proposing this autumn for the Pre-Trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Am I not right this case was subject to Rule 61 proceedings, this indictment, in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, Your Honour. It was the indictment against Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, same indictment. Well, be that as it may, you've had since April last year to prepare a Pre-Trial brief. It's unacceptable now to come before the Trial Chamber and say that you need 18 months, which is what it would have been, to prepare a Pre-Trial brief. It should have been ready months ago. Now, I understand you have problems. We've heard before from Ms. Hollis about the number of documents that you've had to go through. Of course. But that doesn't mean that you can't be getting on with the Pre-Trial brief so that the accused know the case they have to meet and so that the Trial Chamber knows the case which it's going to have to try. You must restructure your work, you must restructure your team. You've got three months and that should be sufficient to do it. By this stage, your case should be almost ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the trial preparation might be more expeditious, for example, if we did not have a fully litigated case. Today, only a few minutes before the beginning of this Status Conference, we received a response from the Defence of Mr. Krajisnik about a number of adjudicated facts and other allegations subject to stipulation, and of course, in the next hours, and the next days, we are in the process to analyse them. Plus we were submitted a number of facts by the Defence for potential and possible stipulation, and we also have to analyse it. This is with reference to Mr. Krajisnik, and this is the latest update about the situation. But with reference to Mrs. Plavsic, let's say that we had last week some fruitful discussions, meetings, with the Defence counsel, but so far, we have not agreed to any kind of stipulation and we are waiting, of course. I mean we understand that the Defence counsel just took over the case, and just took over, you know, the interests of Mrs. Plavsic. So we wait to hear from Mr. Pavich, whether it's going to be a fully litigated case or whether there are some areas of agreement. I understand that both parties are tending to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Piacente, that of course is much to be encouraged. Any agreement that can be reached in order to shorten the case will of course have the Trial Chamber's full blessing. And I'd encouraged you before, and I would encourage you again, to continue with these negotiations, these discussions. But that cannot in any way affect your duty to produce a Pre-Trial brief on the basis, if need be, that this is a fully argued case. As I say, the programme gives you three months to do it. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, again, I mean, the concern coming from the Prosecution bench is related to a professional preparation of the case and the Pre-Trial brief in order to avoid any other delay or adjournment of the case. So what I was proposing, humbly proposing, to Your Honour, was, let's say, a realistic prospective of the Prosecution, which at the end for -- with reference to the, let's say, important aspect of the whole issue, which is the beginning of the case, won't affect very much the scheduled trial date because we will do our best to be ready, but the date scheduled by the Trial Chamber or at the latest, at the very beginning of December of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The beginning of December is not acceptable. The date which is at the moment is the latter half of November, and Mr. Piacente, it must be understood that the Prosecution is to be ready by then. Now, the dates which we have put forward, which I have suggested, seem to me to be realistic dates in order to meet a trial by the end of November. As I've already pointed out, one of the accused has already been in custody for a year. I remember at the very first Status Conference Ms. Hollis saying for the Prosecution that it would take a year to prepare this case. You've now had a year and you're asking for another six months and more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Considering -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think there is much point debating it further. The matter should be ready for trial within that time. I will hear what the Defence have got to say in a moment. But as far as the Prosecution are concerned, that must be the timetable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: I suppose I'm not allowed to propose another scenario of difficulties to you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you can mention what -- Mr. Brasich, I'll hear you in a moment. Yes. What other difficulties have you got?

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: You may argue, Your Honour, that it is not strictly related to the preparation of the trial brief, but still, I mean we're finding a lot of difficulties in the procedure set out by the new Rule 92 bis. Of course, we are in the process and we intend to use, as much as extensively possible, these Rules in order to expedite the case. So we are in the process, in an active process to identify all the witnesses with statements falling within the language of this new Rule. But, Your Honour, please consider that no procedure, practical procedure how to get the statements is being set up yet, and to my knowledge up-to-date, up to this date, no presiding officer has been proposed yet. And as we are talking about 41 municipalities and crime base which includes a big part of country which is Bosnia, definitely our estimation is that in order to expedite the case, we should submit to the Court the biggest number possible on 92 bis statements. And in order to do so, we must be, you know, in the position to get these statements and to get all the -- and to meet all the requirements, and this situation, the current situation, is not helping us very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Piacente, if you have difficulties about the Rule and the Trial Chamber can be of assistance, perhaps you'd like to set them out in the form of a motion or the like and we'll consider the difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: We will consider it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That should not hold you up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: We'll consider it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Yes, Mr. Brasich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I, of course, have just gone on board in this particular case, and I will have to rely on the Office of the Prosecutor's completion of their tasks before I can really start preparing my defences. However, a thought came to me, Your Honour, with regard to a possible solution. The Court, if I read the comments made, is very conscious of a speedy trial situation. There has been a change, a political change, in Yugoslavia. Perhaps if the Prosecution would consent to a provisional release, the time constraints would not be an issue, and I would invite the Prosecution to seriously consider such an arrangement. With regard to the plan itself, Your Honour, as I said, I do not speak for Mrs. Plavsic, but she surrendered. My client has been in for over a year. The experiences that I have had with the other case that I have had the honour to represent a client in, the provisional release has had no problems and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Brasich, with respect, that's a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We hear what you say, and no doubt the Prosecution can consider what is suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASICH
utterances.text: Fine. Your Honour. With regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: With regard to the timetable, I understand you've only just come into the matter, and Mrs. Plavsic, of course, has surrendered more recently, but nonetheless, one would hope that some work has been undertaken. There was a problem at an earlier hearing which was raised about the provision of resources. I understand that the Registry are making much more resource available in this case than they are normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASICH
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. With regard to that, Your Honour, in you schedule, I plan to make some in limine motions. Would there be a schedule in regard to that? We have been served so far by 85.000 pieces of paper. Perhaps we can cut down the necessity of all of those documents with the proper in limine motion. Would the Court like to hear such a motion? That would be my first question. My second question, Your Honour, is I'm an American, July 4th is the traditional holiday. We had last year, that problem. I was wondering if we could move it either a little bit earlier or later so that I wouldn't lose the July 4th weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be one of the easier matters to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As for motions, the usual Rules apply about motions, as to when they should be entered, and I don't think there will be any distinction in this case. Perhaps you would like to consult the Rules and act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASICH
utterances.text: The reason why I'm saying that, Your Honour, is I can't make a motion in limine until I get all the disclosure. That's why I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You'll have to take whatever course you think fits. If you can put a motion in earlier, so much the better. If it has to be later, well, then, we'll deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASICH
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, is there anything anybody else wants to say about the proposals? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I know the Court is pressed for time. Nonetheless, I have some grave concerns that I think must be raised before the Tribunal at this time. I was assigned as Mrs. Plavsic's counsel approximately three weeks ago with the purpose of determining the scope and magnitude of the case against her so as to determine what might be necessary and what might be required for adequate representation. Toward that end, we've had several conferences and two meetings with the Prosecution over the past three weeks, and in those meetings, I think we have determined that the scope and magnitude of this case is greater than any other that has come before this Tribunal for a number of reasons. First, all the other cases that have been tried before this Tribunal. If we look at paragraphs 18 and 20 of the consolidated indictment, for example, to see the detention camps and villages that are listed, many of these cases have been tried over the past nine years and essentially have been rolled into this case. We've had fruitful discussions, as Mr. Piacente has said, in our meeting last week with Mr. Piacente and Mr. Harmon, and I think that going through the consolidated indictment paragraph by paragraph, as we did last week, it became clear that at this time, it would seem that the case against Mrs. Plavsic is going to be a case without holding the Prosecution, at this time, to any commitment. But based on the facts that the Prosecution has at this time, we believe that this case is going to involve a case in which the question about Mrs. Plavsic will be whether she should have known what was occurring during the period of the indictment and whether she should have taken greater steps or more steps to prevent what was happening. I mention that because this is the broadest possible charge that can be made. We're not talking about an individual charge at a specific moment in time, but we're talking about what she knew or should have known more particularly during this period and whether she should have taken certain steps or perhaps even more steps than she did take in order to prevent or mitigate what happened. To that extent, I was advised that behind the indictment there are approximately 3 million pages of documentation. That relates to the basic indictment itself. We spoke briefly about Rule 68 and materials that might have to be disclosed under Rule 68. Mr. Harmon advised me that the documentation would amount to approximately 3 million pages. That does not, however, I think, include an interpretation of Rule 68 that I brought to the attention of the Prosecutors last week and that is whether material in mitigation -- as Your Honour knows, mitigation is considered at the same time that the underlying liability is considered in the case, whether material in mitigation would be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: -- be advised to mind the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I'm conscious of your time frame and I apologise. Whether material in mitigation would be limited to the period of the indictment, we believe that it would not. The reason I mention this fact, together with one other important fact, the indictment, the consolidated indictment mentions a number of other additional facts beginning, I think, with paragraph, I believe, 48 through 67. These are facts that do not necessarily relate directly to the facts that need to be proven by the Prosecution but, as Mr. Harmon and Mr. Piacente explained to me, these are facts that are necessary in order to create the proper context so that the Tribunal may understand the full context in which the Prosecution is making its case. The comments, of course, from our end on that is that there may be additional facts that we feel may become necessary in order to more fully complete the context that the Prosecution may feel is necessary for the Court to fully understand the situation. If the Court would look at these paragraphs, it will see that these paragraphs relate almost exclusively to what the Bosnian Serbs were doing at particular moments in time. It has nothing to say about what may have been done to the Bosnian Serbs at this particular time. The reason I mention this context of additional facts in the Prosecution's consolidated indictment and the Rule 68 is that the 3 million documents and 3 million pages that stand behind this indictment apparently may not even go to documents that may be necessary under a full or more complete Rule 68 disclosure relating to, say, mitigation or to additional facts that may become necessary in order to more fully advise the Court as to the context of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour? With all this in mind, I've taken the time to also meet with the Registrar, and have expressed both to the Registrar, and to Mr. Piacente and Mr. Harmon most recently, my grave concerns about whether Ms. Plavsic will be able to defend herself in this matter, and that's going to depend on whether she is given adequate resources to defend herself. A simple point, Your Honour: 3 million pages, if it takes -- Defence counsel must look at the documentation that's behind the indictment. I cannot, as an officer of the Tribunal or as assigned counsel to Mrs. Plavsic, undertake this case without undertaking the responsibility of looking at the documentation. If, for example, we take two minutes per page - and I'll bore the court very briefly with this very simple proposition - at 3 million documents, that's 6 million minutes. If one person were to take 365 days a year, 8 hours a day, if I were to undertake that, at 2 minutes per page, it would take me 34 years in order to simply read the documents. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you before you go on. I don't know where this figure of 3 million documents came in. My recollection from what was said in an earlier hearing was that the Defence were looking through and -- Prosecution, I'm sorry, were looking through a million documents - still a substantial number - to see what number they had to disclose. But at this stage, there may be little point in discussing whether it's a million or 3 million. I take the point that it is a very substantial number. The important point, if I may say, is to ensure that what is disclosed is what is relevant to the case, and that a large amount of documents are not disclosed which are totally irrelevant. I know there are problems about resources. They have been raised, and I understand that the Registry has made particular efforts to ensure that adequate resources are available to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: May I mention my discussion with the Registry in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Except for this, that this is another logistical problem, I agree an important one, but it's a logistical problem which must be seen to. What are you asking me to do, having regard to the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, this is a logistical problem of such a magnitude that it raises -- rises to the level of whether or not Mrs. Plavsic is going to be able to defend herself. I've met with the Registrar's office. They have made extraordinary efforts in this case to provide resources, but the resources that have been given, which would amount to 8.600 hours, would not even allow us to complete reading the documentation that has preliminarily been disclosed, and that is the 26.000 or 27.000 pages of hard copy. And the 29 CD-ROM disks, that would be approximately another 90.000 pages. And, Your Honour, this is simply -- we are only talking at this moment about reading documentation. We are not even -- this is the very preliminary aspect of any Defence. And so these logistical problems, these management problems, raise -- rise to the level of fundamental fairness and whether or not we are going to be able to defend her. I cannot, in good conscience, undertake a representation of Mrs. Plavsic if I know from the beginning that I'm not going to be able to complete even reading the documentation that may stand behind the indictment. I believe what we have is a situation under Article 21, which created the Tribunal, which specifically indicates in Article 21 that the Defence -- "In the determination of any charge against the accused ... the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees, in full equality:" and, "(b) to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence." As Your Honour has mentioned, the Prosecution has basically had eight years to prepare its case, and has in fact been working on smaller cases that have been rolled into this indictment for the past eight years. They have an institutional memory that we can never compete with. They have an office. They have an entire Tribunal, essentially, behind them. I, Your Honour, on behalf of Mrs. Plavsic, have nothing behind me. I have no desk. I have no chair. I'm not trying now to be facetious, but if we do have 3 million pieces of paper. We have to have a place to put them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pavich, at this stage, you have warned us of the difficulties which you face. What would be most sensible is this: If you gather together the current position that you are in - so roughly what you've said today - explain the position, and it would be better, it seems to me, to put the matter into writing and the Trial Chamber can then consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: I would be happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we will review the whole position. But not only are there constraints of the size of the case, there are also time constraints, as I have mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: This is where the resources become critical, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Particularly with people in custody. Now, we will also find out from the Prosecution the precise size of their anticipated disclosure, and in that way, we will get a full picture of the task which you're facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: I simply wanted at this point, at the earliest possible moment, Your Honour, raise what I believe are very, very grave concerns about whether or not Mrs. Plavsic is going to be unable under the circumstances to defend herself unless some drastic measures are taken to provide either resources or to drastically reduce the amount of material that would be necessary to review. However, I'm not optimistic that the latter will be possible for this reason, Your Honour: The indictment, as I understand it, our Defence and the Prosecution are going to be focusing in this case on whether she should have known what was happening and whether she should have taken more serious steps to do more to stop what had happened. And in that broad context, I think it's going to be very difficult, Your Honour, to substantially narrow the documentation. In any event, I think it was important for me to raise this, and Mr. Piacente may have a comment. I don't mean to speak out of turn, but I do believe that we did discuss this and did I raise my concerns with him last week in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's helpful to have the issue narrowed in that way, and if it is narrowed, one would hope there could be a narrowing of the amount of evidence necessary. Mr. Piacente, I don't want to continue this debate very much longer but is this figure of 3 million an accurate one?

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Brenda Hollis mentioned in the last Status Conference that we were dealing with 2.700.000 pages of documents we have in-house. Of course, the selection and the analysis of these documents is going very, very narrow, so definitely we are not going to submit to the Defence all the documents we have in-house. That's definitely not our purpose. Definitely, I mean, our theory of the case will be specified in our Pre-Trial brief and I'm afraid it won't be the same that the Defence counsel has anticipated. And I don't want to add anything else about that, but definitely our theory of the case won't imply the necessity to hand over to the Defence or to the Trial Chamber such a huge amount of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you will have heard what I said about narrowing, as far as possible, the documents which are disclosed to those which are really relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we asked both Defence counsels of both accused to specify, if they are available, to their potential or future theory of the case or strategy of the Defence. We didn't mean anything but try to understand what the theory of the case might be and try to adapt our disclosure process to that theory of the case, in order to narrow as much as possible and to expedite as much as possible the trial preparation. Also for the counterpart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And are you in a position to say what volume of documents might be disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: I don't want to be wrong, Your Honour, so let me not answer this question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Clearly, Mr. Pavich, what would assist would be further discussions with the Prosecutor and Mr. Brasich, too, in order to try and narrow the scope of the case which would be in everybody's interest; yours in terms of preparation, Prosecution in terms of their disclosure. It may be in that way that some progress can be made. But the Trial Chamber -- I should make this point to both sides, that the Trial Chamber is available, and I as the Pre-Trial judge am available at any time to assist in these matters. And although I've listed Status Conferences, it's perfectly possible to have additional hearings at any time which is convenient, and it may be that that would be a sensible way forward. Now, is there anything anybody else wants to raise at the moment? There is the necessity for the Trial Chamber to inquire about detention. This is the opportunity for the accused to raise issues in relation to detention. Is there anything that anybody wants to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: As Your Honour knows, when I was assigned, an application had been pending for Pre-Trial release. We withdrew that simply to give us an opportunity to refile it and in order to prepare in a way in which I think we may be able to get some additional guarantees. So I anticipate filing an application within the next two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Brasich, anything you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not at this -- I keep forgetting that. Not at this time, Your Honour, I'm too new in the case to have really taken all possible steps on behalf of my client, so I would like to reserve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, this matter will be adjourned. There will be a Status Conference at the latest on the 17th of May, but meanwhile, the Trial Chamber will be reviewing the position, having regard to what's been said here today, and if necessary, further hearings will be scheduled.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at 5.08 p.m.
